Longer sentences have an obvious political appeal: they are cheap to announce, easy to understand and seem to promise that offenders will get what they deserve. As a strategy for reducing crime, however, they are among the least efficient tools available, and I disagree that they represent the best approach.

It is worth being precise about what prison can achieve. Locking up a persistent burglar or a violent offender prevents that person from harming the public for the duration of the sentence, and for a small group of dangerous individuals this protection justifies long terms. But the effect diminishes sharply as sentences lengthen, because most people commit crimes in their late teens and twenties and simply grow out of it. An extra five years imposed on a forty-year-old therefore buys very little additional safety at considerable public expense.

The deterrent argument is weaker still. It assumes that would-be offenders weigh up the likely penalty before acting, whereas a great deal of crime is impulsive, committed under the influence of drink or drugs, or carried out by people who are confident they will not be caught. What changes behaviour is the perceived likelihood of detection, not the theoretical severity of a punishment that may never arrive. Worse, longer spells inside tend to sever the ties that keep people law-abiding, such as a job, a tenancy and a family, so many prisoners are released more likely to reoffend than when they went in.

If the aim is genuinely fewer victims, the money spent on extending sentences would achieve more elsewhere: on visible, well-resourced policing that raises the chance of being caught, on drug treatment, and on education and employment schemes that give released prisoners a stake in staying out of trouble.

Prison has a necessary place in any justice system, but treating sentence length as the main lever confuses being seen to be tough with being effective.

As cities grow, governments face a difficult choice about how to spend limited transport budgets. Some argue that new roads are needed to keep traffic moving, but I strongly agree that investment in public transport should be the priority, at least in urban areas.

The main reason is that building more roads rarely solves congestion for long. Wider roads make driving more attractive, so more people choose to travel by car and the new capacity quickly fills up, a pattern known as induced demand. In contrast, a single metro line or bus rapid transit route can carry tens of thousands of passengers an hour while occupying far less space than the equivalent number of cars. Ho Chi Minh City's first metro line, for instance, offers commuters an alternative to roads that are already saturated with motorbikes.

Public transport also brings environmental and social benefits. Fewer private vehicles mean lower emissions and cleaner air, which matters in cities where pollution is a growing health concern. Furthermore, affordable buses and trains give mobility to people who cannot drive or cannot afford a car, such as students, the elderly and low-income workers, allowing them to reach jobs and services.

Of course, roads cannot be ignored entirely. Rural areas with scattered populations may have no realistic alternative to cars, and goods still need to be transported by lorry. Existing roads must therefore be maintained, and in some regions new links may be justified. However, these are exceptions rather than a reason to make road building the main focus of spending.

In conclusion, I believe governments should direct most of their transport investment towards public transport. It moves more people more efficiently, reduces pollution and makes cities fairer, whereas new roads tend to offer only a temporary solution.

The choice between building roads and improving public transport is often framed as a contest between drivers and everyone else, but it is better understood as a question of how a city uses scarce space. On that basis, I largely agree that public transport should take priority, although the argument applies far more strongly to cities than to the countryside.

The central problem with new urban roads is that they tend to defeat their own purpose. Extra lanes make driving temporarily quicker, which encourages more people to drive, and within a few years the new capacity is as congested as the old. A rail line does not suffer from this effect in the same way, since additional passengers make a service more viable rather than slower, and a single track can carry as many people as a motorway several times its width. For a growing city, the arithmetic of space alone makes mass transit the only option that can keep pace with demand.

There are wider gains as well. Frequent, reliable services give mobility to people who cannot drive, including teenagers, many older residents and those who simply cannot afford a car, and they reduce the emissions and noise that make dense neighbourhoods unpleasant to live in.

That said, it would be a mistake to treat road spending as inherently wasteful. Buses, delivery vans and ambulances all depend on roads, and in sparsely populated rural regions a regular bus service may cost far more per passenger than a well-maintained road. In such places, modest investment in roads, combined with on-demand minibuses, is the more realistic choice. Even in cities, maintaining existing roads is not the same as building new ones, and neglecting repairs would be a false economy.

Space programmes cost billions of dollars every year, and at a time when many countries struggle with poverty, climate change and ageing populations, their value is often questioned. Some people believe this money should be redirected to problems on Earth, while others defend space research. In my view, space exploration deserves continued funding, although at a modest and carefully justified level.

Critics argue that it is difficult to justify sending probes to Mars when millions of people lack clean water, healthcare or decent housing. Public money is limited, and every dollar spent on rockets is a dollar not spent on hospitals or schools. From this perspective, governments have a moral duty to address urgent human suffering before pursuing scientific curiosity, especially since the benefits of space missions can seem distant and abstract to ordinary taxpayers.

On the other hand, space research often helps to solve the very problems that critics mention. Satellites allow scientists to monitor deforestation, track storms and measure rising sea levels, providing data that is essential for tackling climate change. Technologies first developed for space programmes, such as water purification systems and improved medical imaging, have later been used in everyday life. In addition, space missions inspire young people to study science and engineering, which strengthens a nation's economy in the long run.

I believe the second argument is stronger, because the choice is not really between space and Earth. Space budgets usually represent a very small share of public spending, and cutting them would make little difference to healthcare or education. However, governments should ensure that missions have clear scientific or practical goals rather than serving mainly as symbols of national prestige.

In conclusion, although problems on Earth must remain the priority, a reasonable investment in space exploration is justified by its practical, scientific and educational benefits.

Whenever a rocket launch dominates the headlines, someone inevitably asks why the money was not spent on hospitals instead. The question is reasonable, but it rests on the assumption that space exploration is a single activity, when in fact it ranges from weather satellites to symbolic crewed missions. Once that distinction is made, I believe most space spending is defensible, though not all of it.

Those who oppose it argue from urgency. A government that cannot guarantee clean water or timely surgery for its citizens, they say, has no business funding expeditions to distant planets, and the benefits of such missions are often speculative and decades away. This objection carries particular force in poorer countries, where launching a national space programme can look more like a bid for prestige than a response to public need.

Yet a large share of what is labelled 'space spending' is directed at problems on Earth. Satellites underpin weather forecasting, crop monitoring, navigation and the measurement of melting ice sheets; without them, governments would have far less reliable warning of typhoons or droughts. Robotic missions to other planets also yield knowledge about climate and geology that cannot be gained any other way, and at a fraction of the cost of sending people.

Where the critics are on firmer ground is with crewed exploration. Putting astronauts on the Moon or Mars costs vastly more than equivalent robotic work, largely because keeping humans alive in space is so demanding, and the scientific return per dollar is correspondingly lower. Such missions can inspire a generation, but inspiration is difficult to weigh against a waiting list for cancer treatment.

My conclusion, therefore, is that governments should continue to fund space activities that observe and protect our own planet, along with carefully chosen robotic science, while subjecting expensive crewed projects to far stricter scrutiny. The real choice is not between space and Earth, but between space spending that serves people on the ground and spending that mainly serves national pride.

Childhood obesity has risen sharply in recent decades, not only in wealthy nations but also in rapidly developing countries such as Vietnam and China. This trend has several causes linked to modern lifestyles, but families, schools and governments can all play a part in reversing it.

The main cause is a change in diet. Processed foods, sugary drinks and fast food are now cheaper and more widely available than ever, and they are heavily advertised to children through television and social media. Busy parents who work long hours often rely on these convenient options instead of preparing home-cooked meals. At the same time, children are far less active than previous generations. Many spend hours each day on phones, tablets and computer games, while in crowded cities there is little safe space for outdoor play. In some education systems, pressure to perform well academically has also reduced the time available for sport and physical education.

Tackling this problem requires action at several levels. Governments could introduce a tax on sugary drinks, as the United Kingdom and Mexico have done, and restrict advertisements for unhealthy food during children's programmes. Schools have an important role too. They should provide nutritious meals, remove vending machines selling snacks and fizzy drinks, and guarantee at least one hour of physical activity each day. Finally, parents need better information about nutrition, and local authorities could create more parks and sports facilities so that children have safe places to exercise.

In conclusion, rising childhood obesity is mainly the result of unhealthy diets and inactive lifestyles. A combination of government regulation, healthier school environments and greater parental awareness offers the best chance of helping children grow up at a healthy weight.

It is tempting to explain rising childhood obesity as a failure of willpower, either on the part of children who eat too much or parents who allow it. A more convincing explanation is that the environment in which children now grow up makes unhealthy choices the easiest ones, and any lasting solution must therefore change that environment rather than simply exhort families to try harder.

The most powerful cause is the food on offer. Energy-dense snacks and sweetened drinks have become cheaper, more widely available and more aggressively marketed than at any point in the past, often through games and videos that children watch without recognising them as advertising. When both parents work long hours, convenience foods also become the default at home, not through ignorance but through exhaustion. At the same time, the space and time for physical activity have shrunk. In many cities, traffic and a lack of parks mean that children are driven to school and kept indoors afterwards, where screens offer more immediate rewards than a walk ever could.

Because the causes are structural, so too should be the remedies. Taxes on sugary drinks have encouraged manufacturers in several countries to reduce sugar content, which improves the diet even of people who never read a label. Restrictions on advertising unhealthy food to children, including on social media and gaming platforms, would address a form of pressure that parents can barely see, let alone counter. Schools are well placed to help too, by serving nutritious lunches and protecting time for physical education rather than sacrificing it to exam preparation. Urban planning matters as well: safe walking routes to school and accessible playgrounds make activity a normal part of the day rather than an extra effort.

Education for parents has a role, but on its own it tends to reach those already motivated. Childhood obesity has grown because society changed around children, and it will fall only when the healthy option once again becomes the easy one.

"which improves the diet even of people who never read a label" chỉ ra cơ chế của thuế đồ uống có đường, không chỉ nêu tên giải pháp. Giải pháp được phát triển đầy đủ là yêu cầu TR band 9.

Traffic congestion is often treated as a minor irritation of urban life, something to complain about rather than to solve. Its costs, however, are substantial and widely spread, and the most effective solutions are frequently the least popular ones politically.

The most obvious cost is time. A commuter who spends two hours a day in traffic loses the equivalent of several working weeks a year, time that could have been spent working, resting or with family. For businesses, unpredictable journey times disrupt deliveries and make it harder to recruit staff who live across the city, so congestion quietly reduces a city's economic output. The health effects are equally serious. Vehicles idling in queues produce more pollution per kilometre than those moving freely, exposing pedestrians, cyclists and nearby residents, many of whom do not own a car themselves, to fumes linked to asthma and heart disease. Congestion also falls hardest on the poor, who are more likely to live beside busy roads and less able to move closer to their jobs.

Solving the problem requires accepting an uncomfortable truth: road space in a city centre is a scarce resource that is currently given away free. Congestion charging, which requires drivers to pay to enter central areas at busy times, addresses this directly, and cities that have introduced it have generally seen traffic fall and journey times become more reliable. Crucially, the revenue can be used to fund the second part of any solution, namely fast and frequent public transport, so that people who stop driving have a genuine alternative. Over the longer term, planning policies that allow people to live nearer their work, along with safe cycle lanes for short trips, reduce the demand for journeys altogether.

Building more roads, by contrast, offers only temporary relief, as new capacity tends to attract new traffic. Congestion will ease only when driving reflects its true cost and the alternatives become genuinely attractive.

Reports in many countries suggest that a growing proportion of crimes, from shoplifting to online fraud, are committed by teenagers and young adults. This trend has a number of social and economic causes, but it can be addressed through support from families, schools and communities.

One major reason is a lack of opportunity. In areas with high youth unemployment, young people who leave school without qualifications may see little chance of earning a decent income legally, and crime can appear to offer quick money and status. Family problems also play a role. Children who grow up with little supervision, perhaps because their parents work long hours or the family has broken down, are more easily influenced by older peers or gangs. Furthermore, the internet has created new temptations. Social media can glamorise violence and luxury lifestyles, and young people with digital skills may be drawn into cybercrime, which they often do not regard as seriously as physical theft.

Preventing youth crime requires early intervention rather than punishment alone. Schools should identify students who are falling behind or are frequently absent and provide them with mentoring, since dropping out of education is closely linked to offending. Communities can offer affordable sports clubs, music programmes and youth centres that give teenagers a positive way to spend their free time and build self-esteem. Governments could also fund apprenticeships and vocational training so that young people without academic qualifications have a realistic path into work. For those who have already offended, programmes that make them repair the harm they have caused, rather than sending them to adult prisons, are more likely to change their behaviour.

In conclusion, youth crime is driven mainly by limited opportunities, weak family support and new online influences. Early support, constructive activities and routes into employment are the most effective ways to prevent it.
t2.model9:
Reports of rising youth crime tend to provoke calls for harsher treatment of young offenders. Before deciding how to respond, though, it is worth recognising that much of this increase reflects changes in the kinds of crime available to young people, and that the most effective prevention happens long before anyone reaches a courtroom.

Part of the explanation lies in the internet. Online fraud, the sale of stolen accounts and the sharing of illegal content can be carried out from a bedroom, require no physical confrontation and feel, to a teenager, closer to a game than to a crime. Social media also exposes young people to images of effortless wealth while providing direct channels through which criminal groups recruit them, sometimes to move money through their bank accounts in return for a small fee. Older causes have not disappeared either. In areas where jobs for school leavers are scarce, crime can appear to offer the income and status that legitimate work does not, and adolescents with little adult supervision are especially susceptible to the influence of older peers.

Prevention should therefore start early and focus on the moments when young people are most at risk of drifting into trouble. Schools are often the first to notice warning signs such as persistent absence or exclusion, and pairing such pupils with mentors and keeping them in education is far cheaper than dealing with the consequences later. Youth clubs and sports programmes offer something less tangible but equally important: a place to belong that does not depend on a gang. Online risks call for a different response, including teaching teenagers how fraud and recruitment schemes work, and requiring banks and platforms to detect the accounts being used to exploit them.

When young people do offend, approaches that make them confront the harm they have caused tend to reduce reoffending more than detention, which often introduces them to more experienced criminals. Youth crime is better prevented by keeping doors open than by locking them.

"much of this increase reflects changes in the kinds of crime available to young people" giải thích bản chất xu hướng trước khi đi vào nguyên nhân. Cách tiếp cận này cho thấy người viết phân tích chứ không chỉ liệt kê (TR band 9).

"feel, to a teenager, closer to a game than to a crime" dùng chèn trạng ngữ giữa câu một cách tự nhiên để nêu cảm nhận của thanh thiếu niên. Cấu trúc chèn này là GRA band 9, và ý rất sắc (TR).

"to move money through their bank accounts in return for a small fee" mô tả cụ thể cách tội phạm lợi dụng người trẻ mà không bịa số liệu. Ví dụ thực tế, đúng thời sự là điểm mạnh về TR.

"Older causes have not disappeared either" nối hai nhóm nguyên nhân một cách tự nhiên, không dùng "Another reason is". Đây là liên kết theo ý, đúng CC band 9.

"Online risks call for a different response" cho thấy giải pháp được thiết kế theo từng nguyên nhân đã nêu. Sự tương ứng chặt chẽ giữa hai phần đề là dấu hiệu TR band 9.
Precise abstract vocabulary
"something less tangible but equally important: a place to belong that does not depend on a gang" diễn đạt giá trị vô hình bằng ngôn ngữ chính xác. LR band 9 là gọi tên đúng những điều khó gọi tên.

"Youth crime is better prevented by keeping doors open than by locking them" chơi chữ giữa "mở cơ hội" và "nhốt" một cách tinh tế. Câu kết ngắn, dễ nhớ, chốt quan điểm cả bài.

Bài band 9 đi sâu hơn ở mảng online: giải thích vì sao tội phạm mạng có vẻ "giống trò chơi" và cách băng nhóm tuyển người trẻ làm tài khoản trung gian. Ngữ pháp có chèn trạng ngữ và cấu trúc so sánh tự nhiên, cùng câu kết hình ảnh, nâng GRA và LR lên band 9.

The amount of time people spend on their smartphones is usually discussed as a problem of self-control. That explanation is incomplete, because the device has absorbed so many everyday functions that some screen time is no longer optional, and whether the trend is harmful depends largely on which kind of use we are talking about.

The first reason for the increase is simple consolidation. Within a decade, the phone has replaced the wallet, the map, the camera, the bank branch and, for many workers, the office noticeboard. Activities that used to happen without a screen now require one, so even a person with no interest in social media may spend an hour a day on their phone simply running their life. The second reason is less innocent. The most popular apps are funded by advertising, which means their revenue depends on capturing as much attention as possible, and they are designed accordingly, with endless feeds, unpredictable rewards and notifications timed to draw users back.

This distinction matters when judging the trend. Time spent paying bills, video-calling a grandparent or following a language course is not a cause for concern, and in many respects it represents a genuine improvement in convenience and access. The difficulty lies with compulsive use, the habit of checking a phone dozens of times an hour without any particular purpose. This fragments attention, making sustained reading or deep work more difficult, and when it extends into the night it erodes sleep. It also affects relationships in a subtle way, since a phone on the table signals that the conversation may be interrupted at any moment.

On balance, I believe the trend is negative, not because smartphones are harmful in themselves but because a significant share of the time spent on them is engineered rather than chosen. Asking individuals to resist products designed by experts to be irresistible places the burden in the wrong place, and stronger rules on manipulative design would do more good than appeals to willpower.

In many countries, it is increasingly common for graduates to work in jobs that have little connection with their degree, or even to remain unemployed for long periods after leaving university. This situation has several causes, but universities can take practical steps to improve their students' prospects.

One reason is a mismatch between the number of graduates and the needs of the labour market. As higher education has expanded, more students are choosing popular subjects such as business administration, while there is a shortage of graduates in fields like engineering, nursing and data analysis. As a result, competition for jobs in crowded fields is intense. Another reason is that many degree programmes focus heavily on theory and fail to keep pace with changes in industry. Employers frequently complain that new graduates lack practical skills, such as using up-to-date software, communicating with clients or working in teams, and therefore prefer candidates with experience.

Universities can address these problems in several ways. First, they should work more closely with employers when designing courses, inviting companies to advise on content and to contribute guest lectures or real-world projects. Second, internships and work placements could become a compulsory part of every degree, so that students graduate with relevant experience and professional contacts. Third, universities should provide better careers guidance before students choose their major, including clear information about employment rates and typical salaries in different fields. This would help young people make more informed decisions rather than simply following trends or family pressure.

In conclusion, graduates struggle to find relevant work mainly because of an oversupply in certain subjects and a gap between academic study and workplace skills. Closer links with industry, compulsory work experience and better careers advice would make a university education far more useful for finding employment.

It has become common for graduates to spend their first years after university in jobs that bear little relation to what they studied. Although this is sometimes blamed entirely on universities, the causes are shared with students and employers, yet universities are better placed than either to improve the situation.

One cause is a mismatch between supply and demand. Students often choose subjects that are fashionable or familiar, while sectors such as nursing, engineering and skilled technical work report persistent shortages, so graduates in crowded fields compete for a limited number of relevant posts. A second cause lies in the changing expectations of employers. Many organisations have cut back on training, preferring to recruit people who can be productive from the first week, and graduates whose degrees were largely theoretical struggle to demonstrate that readiness. A third factor is easier to overlook: some graduates are capable but simply do not know how to translate their studies into the language of a job application, describing what they learned rather than what they can do.

Universities can respond on each front. They could publish clear, course-level information about graduate employment and earnings, and make careers guidance available before students choose a subject rather than in the final semester, when it is too late to change direction. Course design could involve employers more directly, through assessed projects based on real problems and placements built into the degree, so that students graduate with evidence of competence as well as a transcript. Universities could also teach students explicitly how to articulate their skills, which costs little and helps those from families without professional networks most of all.

None of this means reducing degrees to job training; a history or philosophy degree that teaches people to think clearly remains valuable. But a university that measures its success partly by what its graduates go on to do will have every reason to close the gap between study and employment.

Over the past decade, influencers on platforms such as Instagram and TikTok have become some of the most persuasive salespeople in the world, often without their audiences realising that they are being sold to. I strongly agree that these individuals should face the same regulations as conventional advertisers, although the rules may need to be adapted to the way online content is produced.

The main reason for my view is that the influence these people exert is at least as powerful as that of a television commercial. Followers tend to see a favourite creator as a trusted friend rather than a company, so a casual recommendation for a skincare product or a diet supplement can carry enormous weight. When such promotions are not clearly labelled as paid content, viewers are effectively being misled, which is precisely what advertising standards were designed to prevent.

A second argument concerns the vulnerability of the audience. A large proportion of social media users are teenagers, who are less able to judge whether a claim is exaggerated. Television advertising aimed at children has long been restricted in many countries, and it seems illogical that a nineteen-year-old with ten million followers can promote high-interest loans or unproven health products to the same age group with almost no oversight.

Admittedly, critics argue that applying strict rules to individuals could stifle creativity and place an unfair burden on small creators who earn very little. However, this problem can be addressed through proportionate measures, such as a simple obligation to tag every sponsored post and a ban on promoting certain harmful products, rather than costly approval procedures.

In conclusion, since influencers shape consumer behaviour as effectively as traditional advertising, they should be held to equivalent standards of honesty and transparency, applied in a way that suits the scale of their work.

Advertising rules exist because people are entitled to know when someone is trying to sell them something. Influencer marketing is the most effective way yet devised of blurring that line, and I therefore agree that influencers should be held to the same standards as traditional advertisers, although the way those standards are enforced will need to differ.

What makes influencer promotion distinctive is precisely what makes it powerful. A television viewer knows that the actor praising a shampoo has been paid; a follower watching a creator's morning routine may have no idea that the shampoo was supplied under contract. The appeal lies in the sense of intimacy, of receiving advice from someone who seems like a friend, and an undisclosed payment exploits that trust in a way a conventional advertisement cannot. If anything, this argues for stricter scrutiny rather than lighter regulation.

The audience strengthens the case. Many followers are teenagers, who are less practised at recognising persuasion when it comes wrapped in entertainment, and some of the products promoted to them, from slimming teas to speculative investment schemes, carry real risks. Most countries long ago restricted what could be advertised to children on television, and there is no principled reason why the same protection should disappear when the screen becomes a phone.

The strongest objection is practical rather than principled. Applying a broadcaster's compliance procedures to a student with a few thousand followers would be absurd, and regulators cannot pre-approve millions of posts. The answer, however, is to keep the standards identical while adapting the mechanisms: a clear, mandatory label on every paid post, the same lists of products that may not be promoted to minors, and the same liability for false claims. Platforms, which profit from this content, should share responsibility for detecting undisclosed promotion.

The principle, then, should be the same for everyone who is paid to persuade; only the means of applying it should reflect the scale of the person doing the persuading.

Banning private cars from city centres was once a utopian idea; today several European cities have done it, at least in part. I support the principle, but I would argue that a ban is best understood as the final stage of a transition rather than the first step, and that its success depends on what is put in place before cars are removed.

The case for car-free centres rests above all on how urban space is used. A private car spends most of the day parked, yet streets in many city centres devote the majority of their width to vehicles, leaving pedestrians on narrow pavements. Reclaiming that space for trees, seating, cycle lanes and outdoor cafés transforms the experience of a city, and the fears of shopkeepers have often proved unfounded: people on foot tend to linger and spend more than drivers searching for a parking space. The health gains are considerable as well, since traffic is a major source of both air pollution and serious injury in dense areas.

The risks of a ban, however, fall unevenly. Residents of outer districts, where buses are infrequent, may depend on a car to reach jobs in the centre, and for disabled people, tradespeople carrying tools and older shoppers, walking and cycling are not realistic substitutes. A ban imposed without alternatives would therefore penalise precisely those with the fewest options, while affluent residents of the centre enjoyed quieter streets.

For this reason, the sequence matters. Frequent, affordable public transport and park-and-ride facilities at the city edge must come first, followed by gradual restrictions, such as removing through-traffic and reducing parking, which allow habits to adjust. Space programmes such as missions to the Moon and Mars cost billions of dollars, and at a time when many people struggle with poverty and climate change, it is natural to question whether this spending is justified. Both sides of the debate raise valid points, but I believe that space research deserves continued, though carefully controlled, investment.

Critics of space exploration argue that the money could achieve far more if spent on urgent needs. The cost of a single mission could build thousands of schools, supply clean water to millions of people or fund research into renewable energy. From this perspective, sending astronauts to distant planets while people on Earth lack basic healthcare seems to reflect misplaced priorities, driven more by national prestige than by human welfare.

Supporters, however, contend that space research often helps to solve the very problems that critics highlight. In addition, ambitious missions inspire young people to study science and engineering, which strengthens a country's ability to innovate in every field.

What matters is that space agencies focus on projects with clear scientific or practical benefits and increasingly share costs through international partnerships.

Arguments about space spending used to assume that only governments could reach orbit. That is no longer true. Private companies now launch satellites, resupply space stations and plan commercial missions, and this changes the question of what public money should be spent on, if anything, beyond our own atmosphere.

Critics of public space budgets make a moral argument that is difficult to dismiss. Every government has to choose among competing claims, and when people lack clean water, adequate housing or timely medical care, spending on distant planets can look like a failure of priorities. They add, with some justification, that grand missions are sometimes driven by national prestige, and that the promised benefits often arrive decades later, if at all.

Defenders reply that space research is not separate from life on Earth. Much of what we know about climate change comes from satellite measurements, and systems developed for spaceflight have found later uses in medicine, materials and communications. Major missions also have a less measurable effect, drawing young people towards science and engineering.

In my view, the growth of the private sector strengthens both positions at once. It weakens the case for governments doing everything themselves: where launching satellites or carrying cargo is commercially viable, there is little reason for taxpayers to fund it directly. But it also clarifies the role that only the state can play. Companies will invest where a profit is likely, not in observing the oceans, studying distant planets or monitoring space debris, all of which serve the public but generate little revenue. Public budgets should be concentrated on exactly these areas, and on regulating a sector that is growing faster than the rules governing it.

Space spending, then, should not be abandoned in favour of problems on Earth, nor defended as a matter of pride. It should be limited to work that is valuable to humanity yet unattractive to markets, which is precisely where public money is most justified.

Admittedly, hosting a major tournament offers several attractive rewards. It can accelerate the construction of transport links, such as new metro lines and airports, which residents continue to use long after the event. Millions of visitors and global television coverage can also boost tourism and improve a country's international image, as happened with Barcelona after the 1992 Olympics. In addition, the excitement of a home tournament may encourage young people to take up sport and create a sense of national pride.

However, these gains are frequently exaggerated. Moreover, the promised surge in tourism is often offset by regular visitors staying away to avoid crowds and high prices.

There are also social costs. Preparations sometimes involve evicting residents from poorer neighbourhoods to make room for new facilities, and public money that could have been invested in schools or hospitals is diverted to projects that mainly benefit international sports organisations and sponsors.

The celebrations, however, tend to precede the bills, and for most host countries I believe the disadvantages outweigh the advantages, although the balance depends heavily on what a country already has in place.

The potential rewards are not imaginary. A fixed and immovable deadline can force through infrastructure projects that might otherwise remain stalled for decades, such as a metro extension or the regeneration of a run-down district. Global media coverage offers a showcase that no advertising campaign could buy, and a successful tournament can lift the national mood and inspire young people to take up sport.

The difficulty is that these benefits are routinely overestimated while the costs are routinely underestimated. Budgets for recent Games have repeatedly ended up far higher than the figures presented during the bidding, partly because cities competing to host have every incentive to promise more and price it lower. Venues built to the specifications of international federations frequently have no realistic use afterwards, leaving host cities to maintain empty stadiums for years. Even the tourism gains are less certain than they appear, since regular visitors often stay away during the event to avoid crowds and inflated prices. There are human costs too: preparations have at times involved clearing poorer neighbourhoods and suspending normal planning rules in the name of urgency.

The pattern is not universal. Cities that already possess most of the necessary venues and transport, and that treat the event as a means of accelerating plans they had already made, have tended to fare much better than those building from scratch to impress the world. It is estimated that roughly a third of all food produced worldwide is never eaten, and wealthy countries account for a large share of this waste. The problem has several causes at different stages of the supply chain, but practical measures by businesses, governments and households could reduce it considerably.

One major cause lies with supermarkets and their suppliers. Retailers often reject fruit and vegetables that are misshapen or slightly discoloured because they believe customers will not buy them, so perfectly edible produce is discarded before it even reaches the shops. Promotions such as 'buy one, get one free' also encourage shoppers to purchase more than they need.

Households are responsible for much of the remaining waste. Many people plan meals poorly, cook excessive portions or misunderstand date labels, throwing away food marked 'best before' even though it is still safe to eat. Because food is relatively cheap in developed economies, there is little financial incentive to change these habits.

Several solutions could tackle these causes. Governments could require large supermarkets to donate unsold food to charities rather than destroying it, as France has done since 2016. Retailers, for their part, could sell imperfect produce at lower prices, an approach that has proved popular in several European chains. Clearer labelling would also help, since replacing confusing date labels with a single, simple instruction would prevent consumers from discarding safe food. Finally, public campaigns and school lessons on meal planning and storing leftovers could gradually change attitudes at home.

In conclusion, food waste results from commercial practices and careless consumer habits. Through legislation, fairer retail standards and better public education, developed countries could greatly reduce the amount of food they throw away.
t2.model9:
Food waste in wealthy countries is sometimes presented as a matter of individual carelessness. While households do discard a great deal, the problem is better understood as the outcome of a system in which throwing food away is often cheaper and more convenient than not doing so, and the measures that work best are those that change that calculation.

Waste occurs at every stage of the supply chain. On farms, crops that fail cosmetic standards set by retailers are ploughed back into the soil or left unharvested, even though they are perfectly edible. In shops, managers prefer overflowing shelves to the risk of running out, since an empty shelf loses a sale whereas surplus stock is simply written off. Promotions that encourage bulk buying then transfer the surplus to households, where it is compounded by confusing date labels, poor planning and portions that have grown over the years. Underlying all of this is the fact that food in rich countries is cheap relative to income, so wasting it carries little financial penalty.

Effective measures must therefore make waste costlier or prevention easier. Governments can require large retailers to donate unsold but safe food instead of disposing of it, and can make supermarkets publish how much they waste, since public reporting tends to change corporate behaviour. Retailers could relax cosmetic standards and sell imperfect produce at a discount, which turns a loss into a sale. Replacing the range of date labels with a single, clear one would prevent much unnecessary waste at home, as many people treat 'best before' as if it meant 'unsafe after'. Finally, charging households for food waste collection by weight, as some municipalities already do with general rubbish, gives families a direct reason to plan more carefully.

Exhorting consumers to waste less has a role, but it will achieve little while the system rewards waste. When discarding food carries a real cost, at every stage, far less of it will be thrown away.

"an empty shelf loses a sale whereas surplus stock is simply written off" giải thích vì sao siêu thị chấp nhận dư thừa. Cụm "written off" là thuật ngữ kinh doanh chính xác (LR), và ý rất thuyết phục (TR).
Following the waste through the chain

"Promotions that encourage bulk buying then transfer the surplus to households, where it is compounded by confusing date labels" nối các khâu của chuỗi cung ứng thành một mạch. "compounded" dùng rất chính xác (LR, CC).
Inverted structure for emphasis
"Underlying all of this is the fact that food in rich countries is cheap relative to income" dùng đảo ngữ để nhấn mạnh nguyên nhân gốc. Cấu trúc nâng cao dùng đúng mục đích (GRA band 9).

"many people treat 'best before' as if it meant 'unsafe after'" diễn đạt hiểu lầm phổ biến bằng cách chơi chữ chính xác. Câu ngắn mà rõ, đúng LR band 9.

Whether at an academic conference in Tokyo or a business meeting in São Paulo, English is now the language most likely to be heard. This dominance has historical and economic roots, and in my view it is largely a positive development, although it carries some risks.

The spread of English can be traced to two main factors. Firstly, the British Empire established the language across large parts of the world, from India to Africa, as the language of government and education. Secondly, and more importantly in recent decades, the economic and technological power of the United States made English the language of international trade, Hollywood films, popular music and, crucially, the internet. Once English became the shared language of science and business, people elsewhere had a strong incentive to learn it, which further reinforced its position.

On balance, I believe this situation brings considerable benefits. A common language allows researchers to share findings instantly, enables companies to trade without costly translation and gives individuals from different countries a way to communicate when travelling or working abroad. For learners in countries such as Vietnam, good English can open doors to scholarships, international careers and a vast amount of online knowledge.

Nevertheless, there are disadvantages. Native speakers enjoy an unfair advantage in academic publishing and negotiations, while non-native speakers must invest years of study simply to compete. There is also a danger that smaller languages, and the cultural knowledge they contain, will be neglected as young people focus on English.

In conclusion, English owes its dominance to colonial history and, above all, to American economic influence. Although its global role is largely beneficial, countries should continue to value and teach their own languages alongside it.

t2.model9:
English has become the default language of airports, academic journals and software, often in settings where none of the participants is a native speaker. Its rise owes more to historical accident than to any quality of the language itself, and while its dominance has been largely beneficial, its costs are borne unevenly.

The foundations were laid by Britain's empire, which established English as the language of administration and education across much of Asia and Africa. But empires decline, and English might have receded with Britain's power had it not been taken up by the next dominant economy. The global reach of American business, film, music and, above all, technology meant that the language became attached to whatever was new and influential. Once a critical mass of scientists and companies used it, a self-reinforcing cycle took hold: people learned English because everyone else had, which in turn made learning it even more worthwhile.

The benefits of a shared language are substantial. Researchers can build on each other's work without waiting for translation, companies can trade across dozens of markets with a single set of documents, and a student in a provincial town can, with English and an internet connection, attend lectures from almost any university in the world.

The costs, though, are more than incidental. Native speakers enjoy an advantage they did not earn: they can publish, negotiate and argue without the years of study others must invest, and ideas expressed in other languages risk being overlooked because they are less accessible. There is also a risk to linguistic diversity, as families in some communities come to regard their own language as less useful to their children than English.

I regard the dominance of English as a positive development, because the ability to communicate across borders is so valuable. But it should be treated as a common tool rather than a ranking of cultures, which means investing in translation and in local languages, so that using English adds to people's options rather than replacing what they already have.

"English might have receded with Britain's power had it not been taken up by the next dominant economy" dùng câu điều kiện đảo ngữ loại 3 để giải thích vai trò của Mỹ. Cấu trúc khó, dùng tự nhiên và phục vụ lập luận (GRA band 9).

"people learned English because everyone else had, which in turn made learning it even more worthwhile" giải thích cơ chế hiệu ứng mạng lưới bằng lời thường. Ý sâu, diễn đạt rõ (TR, CC).
Vivid example of benefit

"a student in a provincial town can, with English and an internet connection, attend lectures from almost any university in the world" là ví dụ cụ thể, gần gũi. Chèn trạng ngữ giữa chủ ngữ và động từ là GRA tinh tế.

"Native speakers enjoy an advantage they did not earn" diễn đạt ngắn gọn bản chất bất công. Cụm "did not earn" chính xác và có sức nặng hơn "unfair advantage" (LR).

"a common tool rather than a ranking of cultures" và "adds to people's options rather than replacing what they already have" đưa ra nguyên tắc định hướng. Kết bài có ý mới, rõ quan điểm (TR).

In many modern families, parents do almost all the housework themselves, either because they are short of time or because they want their children to concentrate on their studies. However, I strongly agree that children should be expected to help with household tasks from an early age, as long as these tasks are suited to their age.

The most important benefit is that chores teach practical life skills. A teenager who has regularly cooked simple meals, washed clothes and managed a small budget will cope far better when leaving home for university or work than one who has never done so. These abilities are rarely taught at school, so the family home is the natural place to learn them.

Household responsibilities also develop valuable personal qualities. When children are given a regular duty, such as setting the table or feeding a pet, they learn that their actions affect other people and that the household functions only when everyone contributes. This sense of responsibility and cooperation is likely to benefit them later in teamwork at school and in the workplace.

Some parents argue that children today face heavy academic pressure and that their limited free time should be spent studying or relaxing. While this concern is understandable, most chores take only fifteen or twenty minutes a day, and they can even provide a useful break from screens and homework. Moreover, sharing tasks gives parents and children an opportunity to spend time together, which may strengthen family relationships.

In conclusion, I believe that requiring children to help at home is beneficial, because it prepares them for independent adult life and builds responsibility. The key is to choose tasks appropriate to each child's age and to present them as a normal part of family life rather than a punishment.

In many households, children's only responsibility is to study, while parents quietly absorb the cooking, cleaning and laundry. I agree that children should be expected to share these tasks from an early age, but I would put the emphasis on why they do so: chores are valuable less as practical training than as a way of teaching children that a home is something everyone sustains.

The practical argument is the one most often made, and it is sound as far as it goes. A young adult who has never cooked a meal or used a washing machine faces an unnecessarily steep adjustment when leaving home, and these skills are rarely taught at school. Yet practical skills can be learned quickly at eighteen. What is much harder to acquire later is the underlying attitude, the habit of noticing that the bin is full and emptying it without being asked.

That attitude develops only when children's contribution is genuinely needed rather than symbolic. A five-year-old who sets the table each evening, or a twelve-year-old who is responsible for cooking one family meal a week, learns that other people depend on them and that domestic work, much of which is invisible, has to be done by somebody. This has implications beyond the family. Children who grow up assuming that someone else will always clean up after them may carry the same assumption into shared flats, workplaces and, eventually, their own relationships.

The main objection is that children today are under intense academic pressure and need every spare hour for study or rest. The concern is understandable, but most age-appropriate chores take a matter of minutes, and they offer a break from screens that many children would benefit from. The real risk lies in the opposite direction: raising high achievers who are helpless at home.

Requiring children to help is therefore justified, provided that tasks match their age and are presented as part of belonging to a family rather than as a punishment.

Most people now read the news on their phones, and while many websites offer articles for free, a growing number of newspapers place their content behind a paywall. Although there are strong arguments for free access, I believe that some form of payment is necessary if serious journalism is to survive.

Those who favour free news argue that access to accurate information is a basic need in a democracy. Citizens must understand public issues in order to vote sensibly, and if reliable reporting is available only to those who can pay, poorer people may turn instead to free sources that are less trustworthy, such as social media posts or partisan websites. This could deepen the gap between well-informed and poorly informed sections of society.

On the other hand, quality journalism is expensive to produce. Investigative reporting may require months of work by experienced journalists, lawyers and editors, and advertising revenue alone has proved insufficient since technology companies began capturing most of the online advertising market. When newspapers depend entirely on clicks, they are tempted to publish sensational headlines rather than careful analysis. Subscriptions give publishers a stable income and make them accountable to readers rather than advertisers.

In my opinion, the best solution lies between these two positions. News organisations should charge for in-depth content while keeping essential public information, such as health warnings and election coverage, free for everyone. Discounted or free subscriptions for students and low-income households, which some publications already offer, would further reduce inequality of access.

In conclusion, although free news has clear democratic value, the cost of professional reporting means that readers should contribute financially. A mixed model can protect both the quality of journalism and the public's right to be informed.

The question of whether news should be free online is often posed as a choice between access and quality. That framing is understandable, but it obscures a third possibility that I find more convincing: that some journalism should be paid for by readers, while the information citizens need to participate in public life should be free at the point of use, funded in other ways.

Advocates of free news start from a democratic principle. Voters cannot hold governments to account without reliable information, and if trustworthy reporting sits behind subscriptions, people who cannot or will not pay are left with whatever circulates freely, much of it partisan or simply false. A two-tier system of the informed and the misinformed would damage public debate for everyone, including subscribers.

Those who defend payment respond with an economic fact: serious reporting is expensive. An investigation into local government corruption may tie up several journalists and a lawyer for months and produce a single story. Since technology platforms captured most online advertising, the free, ad-funded model has rewarded content that attracts clicks quickly rather than reporting that takes time, and subscriptions have allowed some publications to rebuild newsrooms and answer to readers rather than to advertisers.

Both arguments are correct, which is why neither model works alone. Subscriptions sustain a handful of national titles well but are far less effective for local news, where the audience is too small to pay for coverage, and it is precisely at the local level that scrutiny of public institutions has declined most. For that kind of reporting, public interest funding, from independent foundations or publicly funded broadcasters, can fill the gap without making journalism dependent on whoever is in power.

My view, then, is that paying for news is both reasonable and necessary for in-depth journalism, but that essential public information should remain free to everyone. The aim should be a mix of funding models, since no single source of money can support all the journalism a democracy needs.

Linguists estimate that around half of the roughly 7,000 languages spoken today could disappear by the end of this century, as younger generations switch to national or global languages. This loss causes serious cultural and intellectual problems, but there are steps that communities and governments can take to slow it down.

The most obvious problem is the loss of cultural heritage. A language is far more than a set of words; it carries a community's stories, songs, humour and traditional knowledge. When the last fluent speakers die, much of this heritage vanishes with them, because it was often passed down orally and never recorded. Older and younger generations may also find it difficult to communicate, weakening family bonds and a group's sense of identity.

There is also a broader loss for human knowledge. Indigenous languages frequently contain detailed vocabulary about local plants, animals and weather patterns, built up over centuries of observation. Some of this information has proved valuable for medicine and conservation, and once a language disappears, such knowledge is extremely hard to recover.

Several measures could help to protect endangered languages. Firstly, governments could support bilingual education, allowing children in minority communities to learn in their mother tongue alongside the national language. Secondly, technology offers new opportunities, as recording elderly speakers, creating online dictionaries and developing learning apps can preserve and spread languages cheaply. The revival of Welsh, now used in schools, television and public signs, shows that such policies can work. Finally, giving minority languages official status raises their prestige, encouraging young people to see them as an asset rather than something old-fashioned.

In conclusion, the disappearance of languages erodes both cultural identity and valuable knowledge. However, with educational support, technology and official recognition, many of these languages can be kept alive.

The causes lie partly in how information now circulates and partly in how science has been communicated, and restoring trust will require changes on both fronts.

Online platforms reward content that provokes strong reactions, and a confident claim that a medicine is dangerous will usually travel further than a careful explanation of why it is safe. Because anyone can present themselves as an expert, the distinction between a researcher and a commentator with a large following has become blurred, and people tend to trust whoever shares their wider outlook. Once scientific questions such as climate change or vaccination become markers of political identity, evidence alone rarely changes minds.

Some of the damage, however, has been self-inflicted. During health crises, official advice has sometimes been presented with more certainty than the evidence allowed, so that later revisions looked like mistakes or deception rather than the normal process of science. Cases in which research funded by industry produced conveniently favourable results have also fed a suspicion that conclusions can be bought.

Rebuilding trust therefore means being more honest about uncertainty, not less. Scientists and health authorities should explain what is known, what is not yet known and what might change their advice, since a public prepared for revision is less likely to feel misled when it comes. Transparency about funding and the publication of data would answer the suspicion of hidden interests. In schools, teaching how scientific knowledge is produced, through testing, disagreement and correction, would matter more than memorising its results.
